findings.title: Absolute excludes lose filesystem case semantics after rewriting
findings.evidence: crates/blit-core/src/transfers/filter.rs:235 — the first lexical match wins before the canonical spelling is considered. relative_to_root preserves the suffix's typed case at line 315, while fs_enum.rs:213 builds case-sensitive globs. Reproduced on case-insensitive macOS: src/CACHE and src/cache identify the same directory, but excluding the absolute src/CACHE still copied cache/private.txt without warning. Windows has the same suffix-matching problem despite its case-insensitive root comparison.
findings.predicted_failure: A differently cased absolute exclude silently transfers the intended excluded subtree and leaves it within a mirror's deletion scope.
findings.better_approach: Preserve filesystem case semantics in the rewritten matcher, including the wire representation, or resolve literal suffixes to their filesystem spelling. Test case differences below the source root.

findings.title: Canonicalizing the whole pattern fails for glob paths through symlinks
findings.evidence: crates/blit-core/src/transfers/filter.rs:232 — canonicalize(pattern) requires the wildcard-containing path itself to exist. Reproduced with alias pointing to src: copying src/ with an absolute exclude alias/*.txt warned that it could not match and copied keep.txt. The corresponding literal exclude alias/keep.txt worked.
findings.predicted_failure: An absolute glob through a symlink alias, including an alternate /tmp spelling on macOS, fails to exclude matching files even though its directory resolves under the source.
findings.better_approach: Canonicalize the existing literal prefix, preserve the glob suffix, and then relativize against the source-root forms.

findings.title: Windows relative anchors and trailing backslashes are not normalized
findings.evidence: crates/blit-core/src/fs_enum.rs:82 — compilation trims only '/', recognizes only './', and classifies separators using only '/'. resolve_excludes also passes relative patterns through unchanged. Consequently, Windows patterns such as '.\cache' and 'cache\' never acquire the corresponding anchored or subtree rules; the legacy whole-path checks do not match ordinary cache directory entries either. This finding is based on Windows-path code analysis, not a Windows runtime test.
findings.predicted_failure: On Windows, these ordinary directory-path exclusions silently copy cache and its contents instead of pruning them.
findings.better_approach: Normalize Windows separators before anchor detection, trailing-separator removal, classification, and wire-spec construction. Preserve literal backslashes on Unix and add Windows coverage for both forms.
